text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- German government sees budget deficit for 1997 at exactly 3.0 percent. Finance Minister Theo Waigel produces budget draft. More spending on unemployed, pensions, interest and move to Berlin
- Budget of state of Lower Saxony partly anti-constitutional.
- No agreement between Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition and the opposition Social Democrats on government tax reform during parliamentary mediation

- German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT) says export grew by between six and seven percent. But German entrepreneurs loose share of world market. The domestic market still can not achieve brisk exports
- Full sick pay for 14 million workers in 80 industry branches, according to the Duesseldorf-based Institute for Economy and Social Studies (IWS) of the DGB trades union federation
HANDELSBLATT
- German business expects export boom. With a clear increase, German exports remain mainstay if economy in 1997

- Bundesbank says the state must reduce public spending. Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer says Germany and other states wanting to joing European economic and monetary union (EMU) need lasting solid finances
- Interior Minister Manfred Kanther wants to cut sick pay
- Bonn suspends aid for Cambodia
- A court in the state of Lower Saxony state ruled that the 1995 budget of Social Democrat premier and his regional government had in part violated
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- 14 million workers get full sick pay, according to the Institution for Economy and Social Studies run by the DGB German trades union federation
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet decides on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's budget plans today
- Millions of marks of damage after tunnel leading to the future government quarter in Berlin ruptures.

- The German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT) reports that export growth has speeded up in the current year. The group expect an increase of between six and seven percent, weakness of the mark has helped

- Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer calls for reforms in Germany. He says the decisive thing in the discussion about the Europe's single currency, the euro, is to keep a firm grip on public spending
DIE WELT

- Bundebank President Hans Tietmeyer says it would not be enough for any country wanting to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) to keep budget deficit down to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), but that public debt as a whole and the lasting nature of stable finances would also be crucial factors
- Giant tunnel leading to future government quarter in Berlin ruptures. Hopes it can be quickly repaired and will not delay the work
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition approves Finance Minister Theo Waigel's draft budget today

- Row in Kohl's Christian Democrats over the party's new poster, that it suggests that the European Union wants to copy the United States. The poster depicts a map of Europe with the number 14, for the number of currencies and is juxtaposed by a map of the United States with the number one, denoting one currency
- German firms are strong abroad. DIHT German Federation of Chambers of Commerce say weak mark is boosting exports
